chunks: External EMI and its impact on circuits. The question: What about external sources of EMI? How can they impact a circuit?
External EMI is interference that comes from outside your board: radio transmitters, nearby motors, noise from wall power (mains) and static zaps.
Every loop of copper and every cable acts as an antenna that picks it up.
The effects are unwanted voltage added to weak signals, steady offsets from rectification, resets and glitches in digital chips, and sometimes damage.
Connectors and inputs are the entry points.
Imagine rain falling on a yard full of open buckets. A bigger opening catches more rain. A long gutter, like a cable, funnels water in from far away.
Loops and cables on a board collect radio energy in the same way. The doors of the house are the connectors.
Induced voltage grows linearly with frequency.

At 100 megahertz and 10 volts/m, a 10 cm² loop sees 21 millivolts, as big as a 20 millivolts sensor signal; at 1 gigahertz the simple formula says over 200 millivolts, though the loop is no longer small compared with the wavelength so the real value saturates.
Shrinking the loop (area) is the direct fix.
Immunity: how well a circuit keeps working when outside interference arrives. Induced voltage: the unwanted voltage a field creates in a loop or wire.
Loop area: the area enclosed by a wire and its return path. The induced voltage is proportional to it.
Rectification: parts inside a chip pass current more easily one way than the other, so fast radio-frequency (RF) energy turns into a steady offset.
ESD: electrostatic discharge, a static zap with a very fast edge.
Suppose a strong radio field of 10 volts per meter at 100 megahertz hits a 10 cm² loop on a board. The induced voltage is about 21 millivolts.
If the loop carries a 20 millivolts sensor signal, the interference is as big as the signal.
The induced voltage is proportional to loop area, so shrinking the loop to 1 cm² cuts it to about 2 millivolts.
Even if the amplifier cannot respond at 100 megahertz, its input junctions can rectify the RF, so the reading shifts when a phone is nearby.
That is the whole idea: loops and cables collect interference, and junctions turn it into errors.
"External EMI is energy from phones, radios, motors, mains transients and ESD that couples in through loops, traces and cables.
A 10 volts/m field at 100 megahertz induces about 20 millivolts in a 10 square centimetre loop, as big as a sensor signal.
Semiconductor junctions also rectify RF, so a sensor's DC reading can shift when a phone is nearby. Digital lines can glitch, and ESD or surge can reset or damage the board.
So the connectors and high-impedance inputs are where I protect first."
